name: The Treaties That Redrew the World
description: Peace deals, purchases and pacts that moved borders, ended wars and sometimes planted the next one.

checkpoints.name: Pacts of the old world
checkpoints.note: Rulers have written treaties for thousands of years. Egypt and the Hittites swore peace, and Charlemagne's grandsons split an empire that later became the core of France and Germany.

checkpoints.name: Europe divides the globe
checkpoints.note: Spain and Portugal split the new world with a line on a map, Westphalia brought the long wars of religion to a close, and Utrecht tried to keep any power from becoming too strong.

checkpoints.name: Empires and new nations
checkpoints.note: Britain recognised the United States, France sold Louisiana, the Congress of Vienna redrew Europe after Napoleon, and China and Japan were forced to open to foreign trade. At Berlin in 1884 European states set the rules for dividing Africa. In New Zealand, a treaty between the Crown and Maori chiefs left disputes that last today.

checkpoints.name: Peace without peace
checkpoints.note: Peace treaties after the First World War redrew the map of Europe and the Middle East. Many left anger and lasting grievances: Brest-Litovsk was cancelled within the year, and the terms set at Versailles were challenged within a generation.

checkpoints.name: Agreements for the whole world
checkpoints.note: After the Second World War states created the United Nations and limited nuclear weapons. Camp David and the Good Friday Agreement settled old conflicts, Europe merged much of itself in new unions, and the Kyoto and Paris agreements tried to act together on climate.
